name: optic nerve coloboma
aliases: coloboma of the optic nerve head

clinicalPearls: Results from defective closure of the embryonic fetal (choroidal) fissure, producing a sharply demarcated, bowl-shaped white excavation that characteristically involves the inferonasal disc.
The excavation is decentred inferiorly, in contrast to the morning glory anomaly in which the abnormality is central and the disc is surrounded by a raised annulus.
May occur in isolation or extend inferonasally as a chorioretinal coloboma, and can be unilateral or bilateral.
Autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity is described, including mutations affecting the PAX6 and other developmental genes.
Associated with systemic syndromes, notably CHARGE syndrome, renal coloboma (papillorenal) syndrome and morning glory-related conditions.
Retinal detachment is an important complication, often related to a break within colobomatous retina or the fragile intercalary membrane.
Visual acuity is variable and difficult to predict from disc appearance alone, ranging from near normal to severely reduced.
A relative afferent pupillary defect and corresponding field loss may accompany larger colobomas.
reference.pathophysiology: Optic nerve coloboma is a congenital dysplasia resulting from incomplete or abnormal closure of the embryonic fetal fissure, which normally seals during the fifth to seventh week of gestation along the inferonasal aspect of the developing optic cup and stalk. Failure of fusion leaves a defect through which mesodermal and neuroectodermal tissue is deficient, creating an excavated, glial-lined depression at the disc that may extend contiguously into the choroid and retina. The thin intercalary membrane overlying the coloboma is prone to breaks, predisposing to serous or rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Because closure defects reflect broader disturbances in ocular and systemic morphogenesis, colobomas frequently accompany multisystem developmental syndromes.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination and fundus photography to map the coloboma
Optical coherence tomography of the disc, peripapillary retina and macula
B-scan ultrasonography or MRI where a colobomatous cyst is suspected
Systemic evaluation including renal ultrasound and cardiac/ENT assessment for syndromic associations
Genetic testing (e.g. PAX6, and panels for CHARGE/papillorenal syndrome)
Visual field testing and electrophysiology to quantify functional deficit
redFlags: Sudden reduction in vision or new floaters suggesting retinal detachment
Bilateral colobomas or associated microphthalmos indicating a syndromic disorder
Signs of CHARGE association (choanal atresia, cardiac or ear anomalies)
Proteinuria or renal impairment raising suspicion of papillorenal syndrome
reference.prognosis: Visual outcome is highly variable and depends on the extent of the coloboma and macular involvement; some patients retain good acuity while others have marked impairment. The lifelong risk of retinal detachment warrants ongoing surveillance.
pitfalls: Confusing a coloboma with the morning glory anomaly, which alters both prognosis and syndromic associations.
Overlooking systemic disease, particularly renal and cardiac anomalies, by not screening for associated syndromes.
Attributing the excavation to glaucoma and treating intraocular pressure unnecessarily.
Missing an evolving retinal detachment because the colobomatous anatomy obscures the break.
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course, Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Optimise vision with cycloplegic refraction, correction of refractive error and amblyopia therapy in children, as there is no treatment for the coloboma itself
Maintain lifelong surveillance for retinal detachment arising from the fragile intercalary membrane, with prompt vitreoretinal surgical repair when it occurs
Evaluate for syndromic associations including CHARGE and papillorenal (renal coloboma) syndrome, with renal ultrasound and cardiac and ENT assessment
Offer genetic testing including PAX6 and relevant panels with genetic counselling, given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity
Provide low-vision aids and rehabilitation where acuity is impaired
Arrange multidisciplinary paediatric and ophthalmology follow-up
